parent.body:
## Problem Statement

Lev runs many projects at once, across GitHub repos, GitHub projects and Linear projects. AI agents do most of the implementation and post their progress under Lev's own account. To learn where a project stands, Lev asks an agent to write a static HTML progress report. Each report is a snapshot that is out of date in hours, and an agent must spend a long session to make the next one.

Three things are hard to see today:

- Where every project stands, side by side, at one glance.
- Which tickets are blocked, and when the blocker is in a different project.
- Which tickets and PRs need Lev now. Agents post all comments as Lev, so GitHub mentions, review requests and authorship do not show who must act.

When a ticket needs Lev, he must find it, open the tracker, read the thread and reply. A question can wait for hours because nothing told him about it.

## Solution

Project Flow is a local web app that Lev opens in his browser. It reads GitHub and Linear with Lev's tokens and keeps itself up to date.

- The home screen shows every project at once, as cards, as a graph of cross-project dependencies, or as a table.
- A click on a project opens a live version of the progress report: counts, feature map, in flight, blocking chains, needs you, and backlog.
- A click on a cross-project blocker opens the blocking project with the blocker highlighted.
- A click on a ticket opens a panel with its comment thread. Lev reads the thread and replies there, and the reply posts to the tracker.
- A needs-you list and browser notifications tell Lev when a ticket or PR needs him.
- The page updates in place when tracker data changes.

## User Stories

### Starting and configuring

1. As Lev, I want to start Project Flow with one command, so that I can open it whenever I want to check on my work.
2. As Lev, I want Project Flow to read my GitHub token and Linear API key from the environment, so that I do not configure credentials in the app.
3. As Lev, I want to start Project Flow under `doppler run`, so that my tokens can come from Doppler with no extra setup.
4. As Lev, I want Project Flow to use my `gh` login when no GitHub token is in the environment, so that it works on a machine where `gh` is already signed in.
5. As Lev, I want a clear error at startup when a token is missing or rejected, so that I know what to fix.
6. As Lev, I want a settings menu in the app, so that I can change the configuration without editing a file.
7. As Lev, I want the settings menu to write the configuration file on disk, so that my settings survive a restart.
8. As Lev, I want an invalid configuration file to fail with a message that names the bad field, so that a typo does not break the app silently.

### Finding projects

9. As Lev, I want Project Flow to find the Linear projects where I am a member or the lead, so that I do not list them by hand.
10. As Lev, I want Project Flow to find the GitHub projects and repos that I own or collaborate on, so that I do not list them by hand.
11. As Lev, I want Project Flow to find projects from my local checkouts and devkit todos, so that the projects I work on locally appear.
12. As Lev, I want to pin a project in the configuration, so that it always appears.
13. As Lev, I want to hide a project in the configuration, so that a project I do not care about stays off the screen.
14. As Lev, I want a found project to appear only when it has open tickets and recent activity, so that quiet projects do not clutter the screen.
15. As Lev, I want to set the activity window in the settings, so that I control how quiet a project must be before it disappears.
16. As Lev, I want a ticket that is on a GitHub project to count under that GitHub project, so that a ticket synced between a repo and its GitHub project does not appear twice.
17. As Lev, I want a repo with no GitHub project to appear as a project of its own, so that repos with only tickets still appear.

### Overview

18. As Lev, I want a Cards view with one card per project, so that I see each project's progress at a glance.
19. As Lev, I want each card to show a progress bar and counts per state, so that I see how much is done, moving, blocked and waiting.
20. As Lev, I want each card to show how many items need me, so that I see where my attention is due.
21. As Lev, I want each card to show its cross-project blockers as chips, so that I see which projects hold this one up.
22. As Lev, I want a Graph view with projects as nodes and cross-project blocks as edges, so that I see how my projects depend on each other.
23. As Lev, I want each edge in the Graph view to name the blocking tickets, so that I know which tickets cause the dependency.
24. As Lev, I want a Table view with one row per project, so that I can compare many projects in a small space.
25. As Lev, I want to sort the Table view by progress, by needs-you count and by cross-project blockers, so that I can find the project that needs attention first.
26. As Lev, I want Project Flow to remember the overview tab I used last, so that it opens where I left it.
27. As Lev, I want a click on a project in any overview tab to open its project page, so that I can drill down from any view.
28. As Lev, I want a click on a cross-project blocker chip or edge to open the blocking project with the blocker highlighted, so that I can follow the chain to its source.

### Project page

29. As Lev, I want the project page to have the same sections as my progress reports, so that I read it the way I already read reports.
30. As Lev, I want a summary line built from the counts, so that I see the state of the project in one sentence.
31. As Lev, I want a feature map that groups tickets by workstream and theme, coloured by state, so that I see the shape of the project.
32. As Lev, I want the same tracker data to always draw the same feature map, so that a refresh does not reshuffle the page.
33. As Lev, I want the nodes in a diagram to keep stable positions between refreshes, so that the page does not jump while I read it.
34. As Lev, I want an "in flight" section with the tickets that are in progress, in review or awaiting merge, so that I see what moves now.
35. As Lev, I want a blocking-chains section that draws each blocker and the tickets it blocks, so that I see what holds the project up.
36. As Lev, I want a cross-project blocker to appear in the feature map and the blocking chains as a dashed node labelled with its project, so that I see blockers that live elsewhere.
37. As Lev, I want a click on a dashed node to open the blocking project, so that I can act on the blocker.
38. As Lev, I want a needs-you section on the project page, so that I see the items in this project that need me.
39. As Lev, I want a backlog section, so that I see what has not started.
40. As Lev, I want unlinked PRs to appear under "in flight", so that a fix PR with no ticket is not lost.

### States

41. As Lev, I want a ticket to show as done when it closed as completed, so that finished work counts as finished.
42. As Lev, I want a ticket to show as dropped when it closed as cancelled or not planned, so that abandoned work does not count as done.
43. As Lev, I want a ticket to show as blocked when it has an open blocker, whatever its PR state, so that I only see as actionable what I can act on.
44. As Lev, I want a ticket to show as in progress when it has a pushed branch, a started devkit todo or a draft PR, so that started work shows as started.
45. As Lev, I want the tracker's own status field to be ignored, so that a stale status column cannot make a ticket look like it moves.
46. As Lev, I want a ticket to show as in review while its PR's review cycle runs, so that I know the agents and bots are still at work.
47. As Lev, I want a ticket to show as awaiting merge when every open PR has finished its review cycle, so that I know a human merge is all that remains.
48. As Lev, I want a ticket with several open PRs to take the state of its least advanced PR, so that a ticket is only as far along as its slowest PR.
49. As Lev, I want a ticket with no other signal to show as backlog, so that every ticket has a state.

### Review cycle

50. As Lev, I want a PR with a workcell run to take its review state from the run's stage, so that the agents' review rounds count as the review cycle.
51. As Lev, I want a PR with no workcell run to take its review state from the expected bots, so that bot reviews count as the review cycle.
52. As Lev, I want Project Flow to find each repo's expected bots from its recent PRs, so that a new review bot is picked up with no setup.
53. As Lev, I want to override a repo's expected bots in the settings, so that I can correct a wrong guess.
54. As Lev, I want a bot that restarts on every push to count as done only when it has finished on the head commit, so that a new push puts the PR back in review.
55. As Lev, I want a bot that does not restart on push to count as done after any finished review on the PR, so that the PR does not stay in review forever.
56. As Lev, I want a bot that failed or did not run to count as done with a warning tag, so that the PR reaches me and I decide whether to merge.
57. As Lev, I want a PR with no expected bots and no workcell run to go straight to awaiting merge once it leaves draft, so that repos without bots still reach me.
58. As Lev, I want a PR's approval state from GitHub to be ignored, so that an old "changes requested" bot review does not hide a PR that is ready.

### Blockers

59. As Lev, I want native blocks relations from Linear and native issue dependencies from GitHub to count as blockers, so that relations I set in the tracker appear.
60. As Lev, I want body lines that start with `Blocked by`, `Blocks` or `Blocking` to count as blockers, so that the relations my agents write in ticket bodies appear.
61. As Lev, I want those lines to accept full URLs, `owner/repo#N`, `#N` and Linear keys, in any case, with or without a colon, and with several refs per line, so that every format my tickets use is read.
62. As Lev, I want a `none` value and trailing punctuation to be ignored, so that common formatting does not create false blockers.
63. As Lev, I want blocker lines in comments to be ignored, so that quoted or outdated text does not create false blockers.
64. As Lev, I want a blocker line to link a Linear ticket to a GitHub ticket, so that I can express blockers between trackers.

### Linking PRs to tickets

65. As Lev, I want a PR to link to a ticket through GitHub closing references, so that the usual `Closes #N` works.
66. As Lev, I want a PR to link to a ticket through Linear's GitHub attachments, so that Linear tickets know their PRs.
67. As Lev, I want a PR to link to a ticket through a branch name that holds the ticket number or key, so that my worktree branches link with no extra step.

### Needs you

68. As Lev, I want an open ask addressed to me to put its ticket or PR on my needs-you list, so that agent questions reach me.
69. As Lev, I want an ask in a project with no senior to count as addressed to me, so that questions from runs I drive myself reach me.
70. As Lev, I want an ask that names me as the one it waits on to count as addressed to me, even when it is addressed to the senior, so that escalations reach me.
71. As Lev, I want an ask matched by my name to carry a "matched by name" tag, so that I can spot a wrong match.
72. As Lev, I want asks for the senior to stay off my list, so that I do not see questions the senior answers.
73. As Lev, I want comments that record a decision I already made to stay off my list, so that settled questions do not return.
74. As Lev, I want an ask to leave my list once a later comment or the progress comment answers it, so that the list shows only open asks.
75. As Lev, I want a ticket awaiting merge to put itself on my needs-you list, so that I merge what is ready.
76. As Lev, I want a ticket with a need-human or need-engineer label and me as assignee to be on my needs-you list, so that the tracker labels my team uses reach me.
77. As Lev, I want to set the no-senior flag per project and the label names in the settings, so that the rules fit how each project works.
78. As Lev, I want each needs-you item to show the ask as its headline, so that I see what is asked without opening the thread.
79. As Lev, I want an item I replied to after its latest ask to show as answered, greyed out at the bottom of the list, so that I see what I have dealt with.
80. As Lev, I want an answered item to show as acknowledged when an agent reacts to my reply, so that I know my answer was seen.
81. As Lev, I want an item to leave the list when its label is removed, its ask is answered or its PR merges, so that the list empties as work moves.
82. As Lev, I want Project Flow never to change labels, so that the agent who asked stays in control of its own signal.

### Ticket panel and replies

83. As Lev, I want a click on any ticket to open a side panel with its comment thread, so that I can read the context without leaving the page.
84. As Lev, I want a link in the panel that opens the ticket in its tracker, so that I can use the tracker when I need to.
85. As Lev, I want to reply to a ticket from the panel, so that I answer an ask without switching tools.
86. As Lev, I want Linear comments to show as nested threads, with a reply button on each comment, so that my reply lands in the right thread.
87. As Lev, I want PR review comment threads to show as threads with a reply button, so that I can answer a review comment in place.
88. As Lev, I want a GitHub issue reply to post as a new comment, so that it works on issues, which have no threads.
89. As Lev, I want my reply to post as a plain comment with no marker, so that it looks the same as a comment I type in the tracker.
90. As Lev, I want an error in the panel when a reply fails, with my text kept, so that I do not lose what I wrote.

### Live updates and notifications

91. As Lev, I want Project Flow to poll the trackers for changes at a set interval, so that the page stays current without webhooks.
92. As Lev, I want to set the poll interval in the settings, so that I trade freshness against API use.
93. As Lev, I want to refresh by hand, so that I can see a change at once.
94. As Lev, I want the page to update in place when a poll brings changes, so that I see new data without a reload.
95. As Lev, I want the page to open from stored data at once and never wait on a tracker, so that it is fast every time.
96. As Lev, I want a "stale since" badge and the error when a fetch fails, so that I never see old data as current.
97. As Lev, I want a browser notification when an item joins my needs-you list, so that I learn about it while I work in other windows.
98. As Lev, I want a browser notification when a new comment arrives on a ticket that needs me, or a cross-project blocker clears, so that I see changes that affect me.
99. As Lev, I want to choose the notification triggers in the settings, so that notifications stay useful.
100. As Lev, I want an inbox that lists every notification, so that a notification I dismissed is not lost.

## Implementation Decisions

### Stack

- One Bun process serves a React page and a JSON API on localhost. Bun bundles the page from an HTML import, so the project has no separate bundler and no framework such as Astro.
- The browser renders diagrams with Mermaid.
- Bun's built-in SQLite stores data.
- The configuration is JSON in the user config directory. One Zod schema validates the file and gives its TypeScript type. The settings menu owns the file and rewrites it in full.
- The app is local only and has no login.

### Architecture: hexagonal

- **Domain core.** Pure functions with no I/O. The core takes a snapshot of tracker data and the configuration. It returns projects, ticket states, workstreams and themes, blockers, cross-project blockers, needs-you items and their answered or acknowledged status. All rules in this spec live in the core.
- **Ports.**
  - Tracker port: list projects, fetch the changes since a time, fetch a thread, post a reply.
  - Store port: read and write snapshots, seen state, and notification history.
  - Notifier port: publish events to connected pages.
  - Clock port.
  - Configuration port: read and write the configuration.
- **Driven adapters.** A GitHub adapter (GraphQL and REST), a Linear adapter (GraphQL), a SQLite store, and a file adapter for the configuration. Each tracker adapter makes all its network calls through one `fetch` that the app gets at startup.
- **Driving adapter.** The HTTP API and a server-sent event stream.
- **Poller.** A scheduler that calls the tracker ports at the poll interval, stores the result, runs the domain core, and publishes the changes.

### Data flow

- Each poll asks each tracker only for items updated since the last successful poll.
- The domain core runs over the stored snapshot after each poll, and the server pushes the changed results to every open page as server-sent events.
- A page loads from the stored results first, then subscribes to the event stream.
- The browser raises notifications through the Notification API from the open tab. The server keeps the notification history for the inbox.

### State rules

- The states are done, dropped, blocked, in progress, in review, awaiting merge and backlog, as the glossary defines them.
- Blocked takes precedence over every other open state.
- The least advanced open PR sets the state of a ticket. Merged and closed PRs do not count.
- Tracker status fields, GitHub project status and iteration fields, and GitHub's review decision do not count.

### Grouping rules

- Workstream: the root epic, else the milestone. On Linear, the project milestone, which a sub-issue takes from its nearest ancestor when it has none.
- Theme: the epic or top parent ticket, else the scope in the ticket title, such as `feat(ux):` or `[ux]`, else "no scope".
- Grouping uses the same rules on GitHub repos, GitHub projects and Linear projects.

### Review cycle rules

- A PR with a workcell run takes its state from the run's progress comment. The PR is in review at stage 5 or earlier. It is awaiting merge when the merge ask is open, or when the run ended at its final report with the PR still open.
- A PR with no workcell run uses its repo's expected bots. The defaults come from bots that reviewed the repo's recent merged PRs. The configuration can override the list.
- Each known bot has a done rule:
  - Grok: its review check on the head commit completed, and a review on the head commit exists. A new push restarts it.
  - Codex: its summary comment shows a completed review, and the bot's "in progress" reaction is absent. Any reviewed commit counts.
  - Greptile: no Greptile check runs on the head commit, and its summary comment exists. Any reviewed commit counts.
- A bot that failed, was cancelled, was skipped or hit a usage limit counts as done and adds a warning tag to the PR.
- A PR with no expected bots and no workcell run is awaiting merge once it is out of draft.

### Blocker rules

- Blockers are the union of native relations on both trackers and body lines.
- A body line starts with `Blocked by`, `Blocks` or `Blocking`, in any case, with an optional colon. Bold markup or a list bullet may come first.
- A line holds comma-separated refs: full GitHub or Linear URLs, `owner/repo#N`, `#N` for the same repo, or a Linear key. The parser strips trailing punctuation and ignores `none`.
- Comments are not read for blockers.

### PR-to-ticket links

- GitHub closing references and the linked-development field.
- Linear's GitHub PR attachments.
- A branch name that holds the ticket number or key.
- A PR with none of these links is an unlinked PR.

### Needs-you rules

- An item needs you when any of these is true:
  - It has an open ask addressed to Lev.
  - It is awaiting merge.
  - It has a configured need-human or need-engineer label, and Lev is its assignee.
- An ask is a comment that holds a workcell ask marker. Only the newest comment with a given ask ID counts.
- An ask is open until a later comment quotes its ID or starts with a senior or answer prefix, or the progress comment records the human picks after the ask.
- An ask is addressed to Lev when either of these is true:
  - Its project has no senior. This is a per-project setting, on by default for Linear projects.
  - Its body names Lev near "waits on", "held for", "left for", "decision", "verify" or "restore", or mentions a passphrase or signing key. Such items carry a "matched by name" tag.
- An ask addressed to the senior in its opening text does not count, unless it names Lev.
- A comment that records a decision Lev made does not count.
- The headline of an item is its ask. When it has no ask, the headline is the ticket title.
- Answered: Lev commented after the latest ask. Acknowledged: a reaction exists on that comment.
- Project Flow never edits labels.

### API contract

The HTTP API exposes these resources:

- The overview: projects with counts per state, needs-you counts and cross-project blockers.
- One project: its sections, its diagram definitions, and the time of the last successful fetch with any error.
- One ticket thread: comments as a tree.
- A reply: posts to the tracker and returns the created comment.
- The needs-you list and the inbox.
- The settings: read and write.
- A server-sent event stream: change events for projects, needs-you items and notifications.

### Persistence

- The store keeps the latest snapshot per project, the domain results, the seen state per item, and the notification history.
- The store is a cache. If the store is deleted, the next poll fills it again.

## Testing Decisions

- **One seam: the HTTP API.** Tests start the real app against a temporary store and a temporary configuration file. They give it a fake `fetch` that serves recorded GitHub and Linear responses and records each request the app sends.
- **What tests assert.** Tests drive only the public surface:
  - the overview, project, thread, needs-you, inbox and settings responses;
  - the request that a reply sends to the tracker;
  - the events on the server-sent stream after a poll brings new data.
- **No unit tests below the seam.** The state, review-cycle, blocker, link and needs-you rules are tested through the HTTP API, not as separate unit tests of the domain core.
- **A good test** sets up tracker data, runs a poll, and checks what Lev would see. It does not check internal function calls, store tables or adapter internals.
- **Fixtures** are recorded from real tickets and PRs that show each rule:
  - a PR merged over a "changes requested" bot review (review decision ignored);
  - a Codex usage-limit comment (bot did not run, so done with a warning);
  - a Codex review that left only a reaction (done with no review);
  - a Grok check cancelled on the head commit;
  - a senior escalation that names Lev in a final report;
  - an ask from a Linear project with no senior;
  - `Blocked by:` lines with URLs, with `#N`, with several refs, with trailing punctuation and with `none`;
  - a `Blocks:` line;
  - an unlinked PR;
  - a draft PR;
  - a ticket on both a repo and its GitHub project;
  - a cross-project blocker between Linear and GitHub.
- **Prior art.** None in this repo. The rules port from the `project_progress` script, which has no tests.
- **UI.** React components are thin views of the API responses and have no test suite. A browser check of the running app is a proof step for each change.

## Done when

- [ ] `project-flow` starts with tokens from the environment, or from `gh` for GitHub, and serves the overview with Cards, Graph and Table tabs over Lev's real GitHub and Linear projects (proof: screenshot)
- [ ] A project page shows the counts, feature map, in flight, blocking chains, needs you and backlog sections for one GitHub project and one Linear project (proof: screenshot)
- [ ] A click on a cross-project blocker opens the blocking project with the blocker highlighted (proof: video)
- [ ] Every fixture in Testing Decisions passes through the HTTP API seam with recorded tracker responses (proof: test output of `bun test`)
- [ ] A reply from the ticket panel posts into a Linear comment thread, into a PR review thread, and as a new GitHub issue comment (proof: test output, and a screenshot of one real reply)
- [ ] A tracker change reaches an open page within one poll interval with no reload, and a new needs-you item raises a browser notification and an inbox entry (proof: video)
- [ ] The settings menu writes the configuration file, and an invalid configuration file fails at startup with a message that names the field (proof: test output)
- [ ] A failed tracker fetch shows a "stale since" badge and the error, while the page still renders from stored data (proof: test output and screenshot)

## Stop and ask if

- A rule in this spec gives a wrong result on real tracker data.
- A tracker API lacks a field that a rule needs.
- The work needs any tracker write other than a reply.

## Out of scope

- Webhooks and tunnels. Polling is the only sync.
- Daily snapshots and progress-over-time charts.
- A banner for account or billing failures that stop CI.
- Permission prompts that wait inside an agent session.
- An addressee field in the ask marker, such as `to=lev`. This waits for a convention change in workcell.
- Telling the agents about new conventions.
- Edits to tracker data other than posting replies: no label, state, assignee or field changes.
- Hosting, login, and use by more than one person.
- Changes to the `project_progress` script. Project Flow ports its rules and leaves the script as it is.
- An LLM-written summary. Every summary comes from the numbers.

## Context

- `GLOSSARY.md` holds the terms this spec uses. Read it before you implement.
- The rules for asks, the senior, and expected bots come from a study of real comments and PRs in Lev's repos and Linear projects. The prose rules for name matches are the most fragile part. A later addressee field in the ask marker can replace them.
- Every manager, senior and PM agent posts as Lev's account. No rule may depend on the comment or review author to tell Lev from an agent.
- The visual mockups for the three overview layouts are in the brainstorming session files and are not part of the repo.

subIssues.body:
`project-flow` starts, reads `GITHUB_TOKEN` (else `gh auth token`), loads and validates the JSON configuration, polls one configured GitHub repo, stores the snapshot in SQLite, and serves the Cards view with one card: done, dropped and backlog counts. Sets up the hexagonal layout (domain core, tracker, store, clock and configuration ports, GitHub and SQLite adapters, HTTP adapter) and the HTTP-seam test harness with an injected `fetch` and recorded responses.

## Done when

- [ ] `project-flow` serves a card for a configured repo with correct done, dropped and backlog counts (proof: screenshot)
- [ ] A missing or rejected token stops startup with a message naming the token (proof: test output)
- [ ] An invalid configuration file stops startup with a message naming the field (proof: test output)
- [ ] The HTTP-seam harness runs a test against recorded GitHub responses (proof: test output of `bun test`)

## Context

Parent: https://github.com/AbysmalBiscuit/project-flow/issues/1

A configured Linear project appears as a card next to GitHub projects, with the same counts, through a Linear adapter behind the tracker port. `LINEAR_API_KEY` comes from the environment.

## Done when

- [ ] A configured Linear project shows a card with correct counts (proof: screenshot)
- [ ] Recorded Linear responses drive the same state counts through the HTTP seam (proof: test output)

## Context

Parent: https://github.com/AbysmalBiscuit/project-flow/issues/1
